citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, December). Building Blocks. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Building Blocks multi-context implementation pattern: whole-group, small-group, centers, computer activities, and family letters
description: The curriculum distributes mathematics learning across several classroom contexts: whole-group instruction during circle time (approximately 5–15 minutes, four or five times per week), small-group instruction with 3 to 6 children (approximately 10–15 minutes, two or three times per week), hands-on center activities, and computer activities that "automatically adjust when children progress well or need additional help." Weekly family/caregiver letters describe the mathematics and home activities. This pattern lets teachers adapt activities to children's developmental levels while other children work independently.
requirements: Teachers used the Teacher’s Edition to locate relevant activities.
Teachers received 4–8 full days of initial training, monthly 2-hour refresher classes, and on-site coaching 1–2 times a month.
constraints: Center activities were mostly free-choice, so frequency and duration varied; the content and duration of professional development varied across the studies.
target_learners: preschool children
target_learning_goals: early mathematics knowledge aligned to learning trajectories
examples: In the three contributing studies, children in the comparison group were taught by teachers who did not participate in Building Blocks training and did not implement the Building Blocks sessions.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, December). Building Blocks. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/733

article_title: Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts
citation: Christina Luke and Viki M. Young. (2020). Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Build awareness and educator buy-in before embedding micro-credentials in professional learning systems
description: Introducing micro-credentials into an existing professional learning system can be jarring if educators are not involved. District administrators learned they needed to build awareness of what micro-credentials are, how they are assessed, and their rigor, and to encourage buy-in through clear communication about purpose and value plus tangible supports such as planning time, stipends, and recertification credit.
requirements: Clear communication about the purpose and value of pursuing micro-credentials and tangible support for educators
target_learners: K-12 classroom teachers and district administrators
target_learning_goals: Effective adoption of competency-based professional learning
examples: Districts offered incentives including planning and collaboration time, stipends for preparing or earning micro-credentials, leadership opportunities, and hours toward recertification.
key_sources: Christina Luke and Viki M. Young. (2020). Integrating Micro-credentials into Professional Learning: Lessons from Five Districts. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/8960df64-de36-4121-8af2-651b343b0884

article_title: Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools
citation: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Build a committed staff qualified to carry out school improvement
description: The school leader must build a staff committed to the improvement goals and qualified to carry them out, which "may require changes in staff, such as releasing, replacing, or redeploying staff who are not fully committed." The guide advises assessing staff strengths and weaknesses and recruiting specialists such as interventionists, reading specialists, and instructional coaches.
requirements: Assess staff strengths and weaknesses; redeploy staff with valuable skills but ineffective current roles; replace staff who actively resist turnaround efforts; recruit new staff with needed specialized skills
target_learners: students in chronically low-performing K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: ensuring instruction is delivered by committed, qualified staff
examples: The checklist recommends redeploying staff members who have valuable skills but are not effective in their current role and replacing staff who actively resist the turnaround

article_title: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade
citation: The Conceptual Basis for Fractions. (2011). Developed at least in part with Federal funds from the U.S. Department of Education under contract number ED-PEP-11-C-0068. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/
title: Build early fraction concepts on children's informal understanding of sharing and proportionality
description: This principle holds that primary-grade teachers should treat children's everyday knowledge of sharing and proportionality as the foundation for formal fraction instruction. The presentation states that "Young children come to school with an informal understanding of sharing and proportionality" and that teachers "can build on that informal understanding to develop fraction concepts." It frames effective learning as connecting new ideas to what children already understand in real-world contexts.
requirements: Teachers in the primary grades pose sharing problems drawn from familiar real-world contexts
target_learners: primary-grade students (K-2) before formal fraction instruction
target_learning_goals: initial fraction concepts
equal sharing
proportional relationships
examples: A first-grade teacher asks students to divide 12 pretzels equally among four friends, with some children drawing pictures and others counting out pretzels one by one

article_title: College Readiness Indicator Systems Resource Series
citation: Annenberg Institute for School Reform, Brown University; John W. Gardner Center for Youth and their Communities, Stanford University; & University of Chicago Consortium on Chicago School Research. (2014). Beyond college eligibility: A new framework for promoting college readiness. College Readiness Indicator Systems Resource Series. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu
title: Build adult capacity to collect, use, and act on data when implementing a college readiness indicator system
description: Beyond valid indicators, an effective college readiness indicator system requires attending to the supports adults in the system need. Administrators and teachers need time to reflect on data meaning and interpret complex relationships; teachers may need training on new student information systems; and a data coach can facilitate staff conversations about data. The document notes districts must "assess and respond to data infrastructure needs, and assign staff roles and responsibilities associated with indicators."
requirements: Time for staff to reflect on data meaning and limitations
Training on data systems where capacity is lacking
constraints: Data quality concerns may exist, such as schools collecting attendance data in different ways; internal politics and resistance to change can be bottlenecks
target_learners: high school students, via the adults who support them
target_learning_goals: college readiness through effective district and school data use
examples: The document cites a districtwide culture of data use already in place as a system-level strength supporting the transition from data to action

article_title: Readiness for College
citation: Jenny Nagaoka, Camille A. Farrington, Melissa Roderick, Elaine Allensworth, Tasha Seneca Keyes, David W. Johnson, and Nicole O. Beechum. (2013). Readiness for College: The Role of Noncognitive Factors and Context. VUE (Voices in Urban Education), Fall 2013. https://www.annenberginstitute.org
title: Build perseverance indirectly through mindsets, skills, and learning strategies rather than by assigning more or harder work
description: The article advises that because perseverance is not directly malleable, educators should not try to increase it by assigning large amounts of homework or particularly challenging tasks — such strategies "are not supported by research." Instead, they can raise perseverance by "affecting students’ beliefs and mindsets about their academic work," increasing academic skills, and helping students develop learning strategies that make effort more effective.
requirements: Interventions target the mechanisms the framework keeps distinct: mindsets, academic skills, and learning strategies
constraints: Research suggests perseverance is a trait that is not directly malleable and depends considerably on context
target_learners: adolescents
college students
target_learning_goals: academic perseverance
academic behaviors
academic performance
examples: The article warns against assigning large amounts of homework problems or particularly challenging tasks as perseverance-building strategies, noting these are not supported by research

article_title: School Improvement with External Partners
citation: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf
title: Urban school improvement should prioritize building human resources over adopting specific practices
description: This principle holds that effective school improvement places major emphasis on developing the capacities of people within schools and sustaining long-term support from partner organizations, rather than primarily on importing specific programs or strategies. The report's findings across nine partners suggest that without committed, sustained human relationships, externally promoted practices do not take root. As the authors state, improvement requires 'building on human resources both within schools and in assisting partner organizations over the long term.'
requirements: Long-term commitment from supporting organizations and funders
Sustained relationships between partners and school staff
constraints: Adopting specific practices alone is insufficient without parallel investment in human capacity
target_learners: K-12 students in urban public schools
target_learning_goals: Sustainable school-wide improvement in teaching quality and student learning
examples: The report's recommendation emerges from cross-case findings that partner success depended on sustained relationships with willing teachers rather than on program fidelity alone
key_sources: Fred M. Newmann, Karin Sconzert. (2000). School Improvement with External Partners. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://ccsr.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/publications/ExternalPartners.pdf

article_title: Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings
citation: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Business plan creation and competition as the culminating centerpiece of NFTE entrepreneurship courses
description: NFTE's classroom programs culminate in each student creating and presenting a business plan, which the report calls "the centerpiece of the program." Students identify a business idea and develop the plan throughout the program, including a marketing strategy aligned with their interests and abilities. At the end, students compete for seed money through competitions that progress from classroom to regional to national levels, practicing public speaking and receiving advice from professional judges.
requirements: A NFTE-certified teacher leading one of NFTE's curricula over a semester or full school year
constraints: Classroom programs are delivered during the school day and embedded in pre-existing required or elective courses
target_learners: middle and high school students in under-resourced schools
target_learning_goals: entrepreneurship knowledge and skills, public speaking, and business planning
examples: Classroom programs include experiential activities such as the Buying and Selling Event field trip, the Product Innovation Game, and Community Walks alongside the business plan work
key_sources: Nakamoto, J. & Rice, J. (2017). Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) 2016 Alumni Survey Findings. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED582976

article_title: Supporting Principals' Learning: Key Features of Effective Programs
citation: Sutcher, L., Podolsky, A., & Espinoza, D. (2017). Supporting principals' learning: Key features of effective programs. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/supporting-principals-learning
title: Four building blocks of high-quality principal preparation and professional development programs
description: The report proposes a framework of four building blocks for effective principal preparation and professional development: organizational partnerships between programs and districts, program structures such as cohorts and networks, meaningful and authentic learning opportunities, and learning content focused on instruction, collegial organizations, and data use. The authors state that "Research points to several key building blocks of such programs," derived from a review of studies connecting program components to improved school outcomes such as student learning, principal and teacher retention, and school climate.
requirements: Programs must be built on strong working relationships between the district and the preparation or training program, which the report says provide "a foundation for the other features of effective programs"
constraints: The framework summarizes features associated with positive outcomes in studies published within the past two decades, not experimentally isolated causal components
target_learners: aspiring principals
practicing school principals
target_learning_goals: instructional leadership
school improvement leadership
creating collegial school organizations
examples: Figure 1 depicts the building blocks as partnerships, cohorts and networks for collegial learning, applied learning, and a focus on instruction, organizations, and using data for change
key_sources: Sutcher, L., Podolsky, A., & Espinoza, D. (2017). Supporting principals' learning: Key features of effective programs. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/supporting-principals-learning

article_title: When AI Is Wrong on Purpose: How Students Respond to Buggy GenAI Code
citation: Victor-Alexandru Pădurean, Kaitlin Riegel, Alkis Gotovos, Jyotika Mahapatra, Ahana Ghosh, Paul Denny, Juho Leinonen, James Prather, and Adish Singla. 2026. When AI Is Wrong on Purpose: How Students Respond to Buggy GenAI Code. Proceedings of the ACM Conference on International Computing Education Research Vol. 1 (ICER 2026 Vol. 1). https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811667
title: Deliberate bug injection into correct GenAI code to create code review opportunities
description: A pedagogical design pattern where realistic, runnable bugs are deliberately injected into otherwise correct GenAI-generated code, requiring students to read and repair generated outputs rather than passively accepting them. The design creates structured opportunities for students to inspect generated code, verify its behavior, and make localized repairs. Injected bugs are small, realistic, and accompanied by feedback mirroring authentic development workflows. The pattern addresses the problem that modern models often produce correct solutions for CS1-level tasks, reducing students' incentive to closely inspect outputs.
requirements: A GenAI code-generation workflow with hidden tests
A validation mechanism ensuring injected bugs compile and fail tests
Explicit warnings to students that the model is likely to make mistakes
constraints: Not intended to undermine students' trust in GenAI or their own abilities
Injected bugs are introduced only after the assistant first produces a correct solution, so comparisons with natural bugs reflect response context rather than causal difficulty
target_learners: introductory programming (CS1) students
target_learning_goals: code review and verification
debugging near-miss solutions
critical evaluation of AI-generated code
examples: In a CS1 course deployment, 917 students worked on five prompt-based programming tasks in which the pipeline replaced passing code with validated near-miss buggy variants
key_sources: Victor-Alexandru Pădurean, Kaitlin Riegel, Alkis Gotovos, Jyotika Mahapatra, Ahana Ghosh, Paul Denny, Juho Leinonen, James Prather, and Adish Singla. 2026. When AI Is Wrong on Purpose: How Students Respond to Buggy GenAI Code. Proceedings of the ACM Conference on International Computing Education Research Vol. 1 (ICER 2026 Vol. 1). https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811667

article_title: Finding Common Mistakes In Modelling With Mathematical Formalisms Using LLMs
citation: Lilian Killich, Marko Schmellenkamp, Fabian Vehlken, Thomas Zeume. (2026). Finding Common Mistakes In Modelling With Mathematical Formalisms Using LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17111
title: Tool-supported workflow for identifying, clustering, and visualizing common modelling mistakes as bug fixing transformations
description: A three-step workflow in which candidates for common mistakes are represented as bug fixing transformations that locally rewrite incorrect syntax trees into correct ones. Step (1) generates candidates with an LLM and validates them algorithmically, keeping transformations that explain a delta-fraction of the data; Step (2) clusters candidates by similarity via a correlation graph; Step (3) visualizes clusters for instructors and CS education researchers. The article frames it as replacing time-consuming manual inspection of large educational datasets.
requirements: A dataset of pairs of incorrect and correct formalizations whose syntax trees can be compared
An LLM prompted with the transformation language specification and algorithmic validation of candidate transformations
constraints: Candidates explain frequent structural differences between syntax trees but are not guaranteed to correspond to actual conceptual mistakes
The prior SAT-solver-based approach does not scale to large educational data sets, motivating the LLM approach
target_learners: CS education researchers and instructors analyzing student modelling mistakes in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: Identifying common student mistakes in modelling with mathematical formalisms such as logical formulas and regular expressions to inform targeted feedback
examples: Applied to propositional logic (6106 pairs, 248 clusters), modal logic (12482 pairs), and CTL (7210 pairs) datasets, using the GPT-OSS-120B model with batch size 50
key_sources: Lilian Killich, Marko Schmellenkamp, Fabian Vehlken, Thomas Zeume. (2026). Finding Common Mistakes In Modelling With Mathematical Formalisms Using LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17111

article_title: Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students
citation: Farnaz Baksh, Matevž B. Zorec, Feiazie Baksh, and Karl Kruusamäe. (2026). Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15239v1
title: Buildability and serviceability as social affordances of the human-robot relationship
description: The article proposes that hands-on assembly is an interaction-shaping variable rather than a hardware prerequisite: assembly establishes the user's stance toward the robot as a co-created artefact rather than a delivered product. It argues that treating buildability and serviceability as constituent elements of the human-robot relationship "reframes assembly as the opening move of social interaction", linking material co-creation to attachment, ownership, and sustained engagement. The framework draws on a lifecycle perspective that treats maintenance and repair as core components of the user experience, extending Design for Assembly and Design for Disassembly principles into the initial build phase.
requirements: The robot must be an open-source hardware platform whose build, repair, and maintenance are accessible to end users rather than pre-assembled or black-box.
constraints: Single-session study designs cannot capture long-term attachment or perceived agency, as the article states in its limitations.
target_learners: university students building open-source social robots
target_learning_goals: technical agency and self-efficacy through hands-on hardware building
psychological ownership of a co-created artefact
examples: Study 2 participants treated the partially-built robot as something worth protecting before any social interaction had taken place, and used affective vocabulary such as fun, engaging, and cool about the build.
key_sources: Farnaz Baksh, Matevž B. Zorec, Feiazie Baksh, and Karl Kruusamäe. (2026). Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15239

article_title: What Schools Need to Know About Fostering School Belonging: a Meta-analysis
citation: Allen, K., Kern, M.L., Vella-Brodrick, D., Hattie, J., & Waters, L. (2018). What Schools Need to Know About Fostering School Belonging: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 1–34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9389-8
title: Improve secondary students' school belonging by building student qualities and changing school systems and processes
description: The article recommends that the meta-analytic findings be used "in improving perceptions of school belonging for secondary students through the design of policy, pedagogy and teacher training". Schools should act on both sides of the taxonomy: "encouraging school leaders and educators to build qualities within the students and change school systems and processes". Because teacher support was the strongest predictor, teacher-facing levers are central.
requirements: Guidance is grounded in the meta-analytic findings on which factors schools should emphasise to best support students
constraints: Findings concern school belonging during adolescence in educational settings; effects varied by geographic location
target_learners: secondary students
school-aged children
target_learning_goals: school belonging
psychological functioning
examples: The authors state the findings may be useful for the design of policy, pedagogy and teacher training

article_title: The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature
citation: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3
title: Building performance evaluation as the broader evaluative framework into which post-occupancy evaluation has recently evolved
description: The review presents building performance evaluation as a broader evaluative framework that grew out of post-occupancy evaluation. As the authors state, "We then discuss the recent evolution of POE into the broader evaluative framework of building performance evaluation." The framework is positioned as the current state of practice for evaluating buildings in use, providing the context within which learning-space evaluation approaches are later compared. The review uses this evolution to frame its critical analysis of how physical learning environments have been assessed.
requirements: Evaluation of buildings in use, extending beyond occupancy-focused POE to a broader performance framing as the article describes
constraints: The article presents this as a framework evolution for non-domestic buildings generally, not as a validated instrument for learning environments
target_learners: Students in higher education and school learning environments
target_learning_goals: Understanding how physical learning environments support teaching and learning
key_sources: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3

article_title: The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying
citation: Peadar Donohoe and Carmel O’Sullivan. (2015). The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying. Scenario, Volume 2015 · Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.33178/scenario.9.1.6
title: The Bullying Prevention Pack (BPP)
description: The BPP is a systematic bullying prevention intervention that fosters learner vocabulary and knowledge about bullying through role-play and discussions, aiming to create "a heightened awareness of the effects of bullying on peers" and a defending culture. It was enacted over a five-week period in each of two school years: Week 1 covered bullying in the school and definitions; Week 2 introduced participant players with improvised role-plays and discussion questions; Week 3 addressed the onlooker role; Week 4 coached confident defending behaviours; Week 5 involved signing an anti-bullying contract. Monthly teacher-led check-ups followed the initial intervention.
requirements: Teacher-led classroom discussions with open questions before introducing literature-based definitions
Teachers coached on BPP implementation
Monthly follow-up check-ups by the class teacher after the five-week programme
constraints: Role-plays were reported as problematic for some junior-strand teachers, with some role-plays described as over young learners' heads or too complicated
Overly long instructions were a common complaint; handouts were amended to concise, jargon-free bullet points
Junior teachers reduced the amount of bullying types and Bullying Circle players introduced to young learners
target_learners: Primary school pupils, ages 5-12, in designated disadvantaged schools
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of bullying definitions, types and participant roles
Empathy for targets of bullying
Confident defending and reporting behaviour
examples: Over two school years the BPP was trialled with 231 male pupils and 13 teachers at an inner-city Cork school, and was extended to a whole-school basis in year two at the principal's request
key_sources: Peadar Donohoe and Carmel O’Sullivan. (2015). The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying. Scenario, Volume 2015 · Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.33178/scenario.9.1.6

article_title: The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying
citation: Peadar Donohoe and Carmel O’Sullivan. (2015). The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying. Scenario, Volume 2015 · Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.33178/scenario.9.1.6
title: The Bullying Circle of participant player roles
description: The BPP teaches that "Bullying is often a group process which can involve various participant players": children are not just bullies or victims but can act as assistants who encourage bullying, lookouts who watch for intervening teachers, or defenders who try to stop it. Roles are fluid, with students playing multiple positions across incidents. The pack uses an adapted Bullying Circle (Donohoe and Dummigan 2015, adapted from Olweus 1993) and asks learners to relate these roles to their own experiences, naming the types of players involved in school incidents without naming or blaming any peer.
requirements: Learners are introduced to the roles and asked to relate them to their own experiences before role-playing
constraints: Roles are fluid; a learner may bully in one incident, be targeted in another, or intervene
target_learners: Primary school pupils
target_learning_goals: Understanding participant roles in bullying incidents
Metacognitive reflection on one's own possible roles
examples: Learners voluntarily described bullying incidents that happened in the school and were asked to name the type of Bullying Circle players involved
key_sources: Peadar Donohoe and Carmel O’Sullivan. (2015). The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying. Scenario, Volume 2015 · Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.33178/scenario.9.1.6

article_title: Doing Time Wisely: The Social and Personal Benefits of Higher Education in Prison
citation: Jillian Baranger, Danielle Rousseau, Mary Ellen Mastrorilli, James Matesanz. (2018). Doing Time Wisely: The Social and Personal Benefits of Higher Education in Prison. The Prison Journal. https://doi.org/10.1177/0032885518776380
title: Boston University Prison Education Program
description: The Boston University Prison Education Program is a degree-granting liberal arts college program operating in Massachusetts correctional facilities since 1972, including the state's only women's prison. It "provides a Bachelor in Liberal Arts degree and annual enrollment is approximately one hundred and twenty (120) students", funded entirely by BU scholarships rather than Pell Grants. Students take one to three courses per term in three-hour weekly sessions over 13–14-week semesters, taught by faculty holding at least a Master's Degree. More than 400 of over 1,500 participants have obtained degrees.
requirements: Admission via a two-part entrance examination and a subsequent interview, with approximately 20% to 50% of applicants selected depending on the year
Funding through scholarships provided by Boston University's Metropolitan College
target_learners: Incarcerated adults in Massachusetts state facilities, including a women's prison and pre-release facility, serving short-term and life or long-term sentences
target_learning_goals: Bachelor of Liberal Arts degree attainment across literature, philosophy, social sciences, mathematics, natural sciences, computer sciences, and fine arts
examples: During academic years 1991 through 2017, 54 women graduated the program, 189 took courses without graduating, and 4 completed degrees at BU after release; 2012–2017 women graduates averaged 12.44 semesters and a 3.33 GPA
key_sources: Jillian Baranger, Danielle Rousseau, Mary Ellen Mastrorilli, James Matesanz. (2018). Doing Time Wisely: The Social and Personal Benefits of Higher Education in Prison. The Prison Journal. https://doi.org/10.1177/0032885518776380

article_title: Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers
citation: Kurvers, J., Van Hout, R., & Vallen, T. (2009). Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers. Read Writ 22, 863-887. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-008-9129-7
title: Build adult literacy teaching on the print knowledge learners bring into the classroom
description: The article argues that effective instruction for unschooled illiterate adults should start from what they already know about print: "effective teaching should be built on the knowledge the students bring into the classroom, knowing more about what adults entering literacy courses know about letters, print or written language can help literacy teachers to adapt their teaching practices to the knowledge and skills of unschooled illiterate adults". The study shows these learners already know the functions and uses of written language and can distinguish writing signs, but lack grapheme knowledge and out-of-context print reading, so instruction can leverage existing functional knowledge while explicitly teaching the code.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of what adult literacy entrants know about letters, print and written language
constraints: Illiterate adults in this study had lived in print-rich environments for years yet had not built a sight vocabulary of environmental print, so exposure alone was not sufficient
target_learners: unschooled adult illiterates entering literacy courses
target_learning_goals: reading and writing in a second language
decoding and grapheme knowledge
examples: The illiterate adults had attended about 60-80 hours of literacy classes at testing; graphemes they recognized best were the first letters introduced in the adult literacy course
key_sources: Kurvers, J., Van Hout, R., & Vallen, T. (2009). Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers. Read Writ 22, 863-887. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-008-9129-7

article_title: The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics
citation: Ayush Gupta, David Hammer, Edward F. Redish. (2008). The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/hlns20
title: Instruction should build from, not suppress, matter-based reasoning about physics concepts
description: Because matter-based reasoning provides essential resources for novices and experts alike, instruction should help students refine and build from reasoning grounded in experiences of matter rather than prevent it. The authors warn that "instruction that seeks to prevent students from reasoning in ways based on their experiences of matter or of ‘direct processes,' rather than to help them refine and build from that reasoning, is likely to be detrimental to their learning physics". This counters the SO recommendation to avoid matter-like analogies and language.
requirements: Instructors must attend to learners' ontologies, as the authors agree with Chi and Slotta
constraints: Promoting one ontological description exclusively could undermine novices' access to productive cognitive resources and inhibit their transition to expert ontological flexibility
target_learners: novice physics students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of physics concepts such as heat, electric current, and light
examples: The authors cite Slotta and Chi's recommendation that instruction carefully avoid any language, analogies, or phenomena that might reinforce the substance-based view, and contest it

article_title: The dynamics of motivation.
citation: Bell, J. C. (1919). The dynamics of motivation. The Journal of Educational Psychology, X(5-6). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=journal+of+educational+psychology+volume+X
title: Study pupils' drives in order to build up motives for school learning rather than merely cater to their whims
description: This principle directs educators to diagnose the motivational makeup of individual learners and to cultivate durable motivational dispositions rather than simply indulging momentary preferences. The article urges that "Educators need to study the 'drives' of individual pupils, not so much to cater to their whims, as to build up those emotional complexes, those likes, desires, aspirations, that will constitute a motive power for the effort required in school learning." In the editorial's framing, this is how the mechanism-drive framework should be applied in educational procedure.
requirements: Teachers must attend to the individual pupil's drives and emotional attitudes rather than assume a learning attitude can be elicited at command
constraints: Part of attitude depends on native endowment and is little subject to modification, per the article
target_learners: school pupils in compulsory universal education
target_learning_goals: sustained effort and a zest for learning across school subjects
examples: The editorial points to fostering a zest for learning by combining and developing pupils' drives as the practical payoff of the analysis

article_title: The measurement of ability in Latin. Part I. Vocabulary.
citation: V. A. C. Henmon. (1917). The Measurement of Ability in Latin. Part I. Vocabulary. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+Measurement+of+Ability+in+Latin%22+Henmon
title: P. E. scale values for vocabulary difficulty via Buckingham's normal-distribution method
description: The article adapts Buckingham's spelling-scaling method to assign each Latin word a difficulty weight. Percent-correct values are converted to probable-error equivalents on the base line of a normal frequency surface, referenced to a zero point 3.8 P. E. below the median, so that equal raw percentage differences near the tails count as larger difficulty differences than near the median. The article states that assuming ability "follows the normal distribution," a 2 percent difference between words remote from the median "is not the same as the difference between par 64 percent correct and occido 62 percent correct." Year scale values and a general scale value averaging positions across four years are produced for the 239-word list.
requirements: Percent-correct data for each word from a sufficiently large sample of pupils at each year level
An assumed zero point in ability, taken as a word missed by 5 out of 1000 pupils (3.8 P. E. below the median)
constraints: Scale values rest on the assumption that ability in translating the words follows the normal distribution
Words not missed by third- and fourth-year pupils have indeterminate P. E. equivalents and were arbitrarily assigned the value -3.8 P. E.
target_learners: first- through fourth-year high school Latin pupils
target_learning_goals: scope and accuracy of Latin vocabulary knowledge
examples: On this scale the easiest first-year word, pulcher, received a value of .3 while the most difficult, conficio, received 5.2; a correct translation of ab earned 1.6 points toward a first-year perfect score of 735.2

title: Reciprocal-effects account of academic buoyancy and adaptability as longitudinally interrelated constructs
description: This supplementary analysis frames academic buoyancy and adaptability as two related constructs whose longitudinal development is mutually reinforcing: estimating them as "latent constructs" with parallel multi-item factors, the analysis found that "higher buoyancy at an earlier time point is associated with adaptability gains later, and higher initial adaptability is associated with buoyancy gains over time". The account treats each construct as an antecedent of the other's later gains, with autoregressive stability paths and covariate (gender, age) paths modeled alongside.
requirements: Requires longitudinal multi-item measures of both academic buoyancy and adaptability at each time point, and parallel factors across samples so measurement invariance can be established
constraints: Applies to the subset of studies with parallel multi-item factors (Studies 1, 2, 5, 6); studies with single-item indicators of either construct were excluded
target_learners: School and university students in the pooled multi-sample dataset
target_learning_goals: Academic buoyancy in the face of academic setbacks
Adaptability to change and uncertainty in academic settings
examples: A latent cross-lagged panel model fitted to pooled data from Studies 1, 2, 5, and 6, with correlated item residuals across time, shown in Figure S1

article_title: Butterfly Phonics: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Christine Merrell, Adetayo Kasim. (2015). Butterfly Phonics: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Butterfly Phonics intervention: phonics-based course-book programme with formal whole-class teaching, small groups of six to eight pupils, and comprehension-focused Advanced Butterfly Reader
description: Butterfly Phonics aims to improve the reading of struggling pupils through phonics instruction delivered in a formal style where "pupils sit at desks in rows facing the teacher", who directs questions at random to check understanding. It is based on course books by Irina Tyk: The Butterfly Book (Tyk, 2007) for beginning and weakest readers and the Advanced Butterfly Reader for more skilled struggling readers. Lessons last about an hour, build and revisit literacy skills chapter by chapter, avoid worksheets in favour of an exercise book as a permanent record, and include teacher-read passages, class discussion of gist, corrected reading aloud, and writing using new vocabulary. A distinctive feature is continuing phonics-style attention to sound patterns of new vocabulary into the comprehension-based Advanced Reader lessons.
requirements: Delivery by trained Butterfly practitioners assisted by trained teaching assistants, with training from senior Real Action staff and the author, plus observation at the Saturday morning model school
Recommended class size of less than 15, typically six to eight pupils
Pupils progress to higher levels only when spelling and reading are up to the required levels, checked by a consolidation test at the end of the Butterfly Book
constraints: In this evaluation the intervention was confined to northwest London where the Real Action charity is situated
Mean delivery time was 20 hours over roughly ten to twelve weeks, though one school delivered it over just four weeks
target_learners: Struggling readers in Year 7 who did not reach level 4 in Key Stage 2 SATs or whose reading was at least a year behind chronological age
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Decoding and single word reading
Spelling and literacy rules
examples: In the trial, pupils were taught in small groups of six to eight by a trained Butterfly practitioner and a trained teaching assistant, withdrawn from non-English lessons, with entry points to four Butterfly classes determined by reading age (Table 2)
key_sources: Christine Merrell, Adetayo Kasim. (2015). Butterfly Phonics: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581118

article_title: Butterfly Phonics: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Christine Merrell, Adetayo Kasim. (2015). Butterfly Phonics: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Butterfly lesson structure: teacher-read passage for gist, direct random questioning, corrected pupil reading, and writing with new vocabulary
description: Each Butterfly lesson follows a recurring structure: the excerpt is read aloud by the teacher at the start so pupils gain the gist and context, followed by class discussion in which the teacher picks individuals at random to check understanding and surface misconceptions. Pupils then read a section aloud with mistakes corrected while the teacher revisits spelling, pronunciation and grammatical rules, and the lesson includes a period of writing using new vocabulary, such as dictation or composing sentences. The report notes this overt teaching of the global aspects of a text "sets it apart from many purely phonics schemes".
requirements: A teacher and teaching assistant per class of usually six to eight pupils
Training in the Butterfly method so the lesson structure is implemented as intended
target_learners: Struggling readers at the primary-secondary transition
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Phoneme blending
Vocabulary and spelling
examples: Four lessons in two Phase One schools were observed by the evaluator covering Butterfly stages 1 to 4 as part of the process evaluation

citation: Christine Merrell, Adetayo Kasim. (2015). Butterfly Phonics: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Butterfly programme entry-point table mapping reading ages to four Butterfly classes and starting chapters in the two course books
description: The Butterfly reading programme is divided into four classes with entry points determined by reading age, measured by an in-house test of single word reading (Table 2). Reading ages of 6–7 enter Class 1 at Butterfly Book chapters 20–30; 7–8 enter Class 2 at chapter 40; 8–9 enter Class 3 at chapter 52; and pupils above 9, with confirmation from informal assessments, enter Class 4 starting at chapter 1 of the Advanced Butterfly Reader. The exact entry lesson is tailored to each group because starting points vary with pupil needs. In the trial, all pupils except two remained in their starting class; two pupils began in Class 2, found the work very easy, and were moved up to Class 3.
requirements: An in-house test of single word reading to determine reading ages
A consolidation test at the end of the Butterfly Book before pupils take on the Advanced Butterfly Reader
target_learners: Struggling readers with reading ages from 6 years upward, including teenagers and adults for the Advanced Butterfly Reader
target_learning_goals: Reading accuracy and comprehension progression through graded literacy levels
examples: Table 2 in the report prints the four entry points by reading age and starting chapter for each book

title: Buck et al. five-level inquiry rubric for classifying laboratory activities
description: A rubric defining "five levels of inquiry that range from conﬁrmation to authentic inquiry", based on the presence or absence of six characteristics of scientific investigations: problem/question, theory/background, procedures/design, results analysis, results communication, and conclusions. An activity's inquiry level is determined by how many characteristics are student-generated versus provided by the manual or instructor. The article uses the rubric to audit all eleven laboratory classes, target the three lowest-inquiry classes for revision, and verify that revisions raised inquiry proportions.
requirements: Each activity must be scored on how many of the six inquiry characteristics are provided versus student driven
Point values of activities relative to total laboratory points to compute inquiry proportions
constraints: No authentic inquiry activities were included in the analyzed course
The rubric removes ambiguity found in earlier classification schemes but requires activity-level analysis
target_learners: introductory undergraduate geology students, mostly non-STEM majors
target_learning_goals: science process skills such as problem solving, data analysis, and hypothesis testing
geoscience content knowledge of rocks, minerals, and geologic time
examples: The rubric classified 386 experiments from 22 college laboratory manuals in the original Buck et al. study, with only 8% rated at higher inquiry levels

article_title: Getting to the Bottom of L2 Listening Instruction: Making a Case for Bottom-Up Activities
citation: Siegel, J., & Siegel, A. (2015). Getting to the bottom of L2 listening instruction: Making a case for bottom-up activities. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 5(4), 637-662. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2015.5.4.6
title: Bottom-up and top-down processing as complementary dimensions of L2 listening comprehension
description: The article frames L2 listening as a series of integrated processes categorized into bottom-up (BU) and top-down (TD) dimensions. BU processes are "stimulus-driven", involving "perceiving and parsing the speech stream at increasingly larger levels beginning with auditory-phonetic, phonemic, syllabic, lexical, syntactic, semantic, propositional, pragmatic and interpretive". TD processes are conceptually-driven, drawing on background knowledge, prediction, and inference. The article argues an interactive combination of the two is ideal and that current pedagogy overemphasizes TD.
requirements: Both acoustic and linguistic perception (BU) and contextual guesswork (TD) must be combined for successful listening comprehension
constraints: Relying solely on TD listening can result in misunderstandings
Focusing on discrete phonemes, words, or sentences risks decontextualizing learning, and a lack of contextual support can disadvantage learners
target_learners: L2 listeners at lower-intermediate proficiency and above
target_learning_goals: Understanding spoken L2 input
Decoding the speech stream
Integrating acoustic perception with background knowledge
examples: The article's Figure 1 represents TD and BU processing directionality across perceptual processing, parsing, and utilization stages of Anderson's (2005) model of aural comprehension

article_title: Enhancing clinical competence in burn management through a serious educational game: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Deldar Kolsoum, Tavousi Seyed Hasan, Ahmadabadi Ali, Rakhsha Mohsen, Khodabandeloo Farnoosh, Froutan Razieh. (2026). Enhancing clinical competence in burn management through a serious educational game: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09970-6
title: Serious educational game for burn management covering eight content domains with mastery-based progression and instructor feedback
description: A serious game developed by a multidisciplinary team of software engineers and academic faculty to teach burn management to medical students. Content spans domains such as "Basic Concepts of Burns", "Burn Assessment", "Burn Diagnosis", escharotomy and fasciotomy procedures, fluid resuscitation calculation, referral decision-making, communication and professionalism, and ethics. Students view instructional videos, answer time-limited questions, and receive automated correctness indicators, explanatory text, and instructor-recorded video explanations; incorrect answers require feedback review before advancing, and progression requires a minimum accuracy threshold of 60% per stage.
requirements: Access to the software platform with individual login credentials during the one-week burn rotation
Multidisciplinary design collaboration and expert content review to establish content validity
constraints: Engagement and effectiveness were evaluated in a pilot phase and a single-center trial; effectiveness may be influenced by alignment between task complexity and learner expertise, including a potential reverse expertise effect among novice learners
target_learners: Medical students beginning burn clinical rotations with no prior burn management experience
target_learning_goals: Burn assessment and diagnosis

title: Integrate multiple complementary educational components into a structured bundle for skill training
description: Following bundle logic, integrating multiple complementary educational components into a structured training program may create synergistic learning effects, since isolated strategies may be insufficient to optimize both knowledge acquisition and skill development. title: Build nurses' AI trust through transparency, clinical examples and training to enhance AI competence
description: The article recommends that hospitals enhance nurses' AI competence by building AI trust through multiple mechanisms. Specifically, "Hospitals can reduce AIU and enhance AIT by ensuring transparency in AI decision‐making, offering clinical examples of AI applications and providing training." This works because trust reduces psychological resistance to AI use and increases perceived competence. Nursing administrators should also involve nurses in AI implementation decisions to foster ownership and trust.
requirements: AI systems must be designed with explainability and controllability so nurses can trust AI despite uncertain situations
constraints: Cross-sectional design limits causal claims; recommendations derive from correlational mediation findings

title: Basic Units of Knowledge (BUKs): Content and Q&A lesson building blocks
description: BUKs are the atomic chunks of knowledge delivered in lessons, each referring to a single Medical_Concept via the refers_to_concept property. The article defines two types: "The first is a Content BUK, which delivers definitions of clinical concepts using different modalities. The second is a Q&A (Question and Answer) BUK, which is delivered in the form of multiple-choice questions." BUKs carry properties for VARK learning style, required comprehension level (low, medium, or high), and a simplified two-level Bloom taxonomy, and are specialized by themes such as dosage, side effects, and diet restrictions.
requirements: BUKs are fixed and need to be developed in advance for different comprehension levels
constraints: Q&A BUKs are available only in A or R modes, while Content BUKs can be presented in any of the VARK modes
target_learners: patients with varying comprehension levels and VARK learning styles
target_learning_goals: condition and treatment knowledge at lower-order and higher-order Bloom levels
examples: A BUK referring to anticoagulation medication contains a {treatment} variable replaced with a specific medication name such as warfarin when presented to a patient
